label: 1 Timothy 1:5–7
text:
The word behind ‘commandment’ here isn’t entolē (the word for one of the Ten Commandments) but paraggelia, the noun cousin of the verb Paul used for ‘charge’ back in verse 3 — the definite article ties the phrase back to it, so this reads ‘the aim (telos) of that charge.’

The goal of Paul’s charge to Timothy is love — agapē, the word John uses for God’s love for the world, not the pale ‘charity’ of the old translation. It flows from a good conscience: agathos describes something whole and functioning as it should, producing a sense of well-being rather than the nagging discomfort of guilt.

Faith here is anupokritos, ‘unfeigned’ — built on the verb behind ‘hypocrite,’ the actor’s word for playing a part on a Greek stage; put the alpha of negation on it and you get faith that isn’t a performance. Some have missed this mark entirely (astocheō, an archer’s term for a bad shot) and been wrenched off course — ektrepō is medical language for a dislocated limb, a joint twisted out of its socket, not a minor stumble but a real derangement.

What they wanted instead was to be nomodidaskaloi, ‘law-teachers,’ one compound word — professional specialists in the Mosaic law, though by Paul’s account they don’t even understand the terms they use so confidently.
translation: Now the aim of the charge is love out of a clean heart and a good conscience and faith not play-acted — some, having missed the mark, have been wrenched out of joint into empty talk, wanting to be law-teachers, though they understand neither what they are saying nor the matters they insist on so confidently.

label: 1 Timothy 1:8–11
text:
Paul calls the law kalos, ‘good’ — a word that leans toward goodness as displayed outwardly, fitting since he’s about to describe what the law is good for.

It isn’t legislated for the naturally upright but for the anupotaktos, the ‘unruly’ — literally one who refuses to be brought under, still under law’s authority but resisting it, distinct from the anomos who denies having any law over him at all.

‘Profane’ is bebēlos, built on the word for a threshold: it names someone who has made himself common ground, open for anyone to walk across, because he has kept no part of himself set apart for God — the opposite of holy, not because he’s especially wicked but because he’s kept nothing back.

Over against this whole list stands ‘sound teaching’ — hugiainō is the ordinary word for bodily health, so Paul is picturing doctrine as either healthy or diseased, not merely correct or incorrect.
translation: We know that the law is good if a person uses it lawfully — realizing this, that law is not laid down for a law-abiding person but for the lawless and the unruly, for the irreverent and the sinful, for the unholy and the common, for those who strike father and strike mother, for man-killers, for the sexually immoral, for those who lie with men, for slave-traders, for liars, for those who swear falsely, and for whatever else stands opposed to healthy teaching, according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.

label: 1 Timothy 1:12–14
text:
‘I thank’ renders a present tense that’s really a state: ‘I have constant gratitude,’ not a one-time acknowledgment but Paul’s settled disposition.

The verb behind ‘enabled’ is the same one he uses in Philippians 4:13 — literally ‘clothed with strength,’ picturing God dressing him in a capacity he didn’t have on his own, here specifically the strength to carry the gospel he’d once tried to destroy.

‘Counted’ is hēgeomai, a word for a weighed, deliberate judgment based on evidence, not a gut feeling — God looked at the zeal Paul had poured into persecuting the church and judged, correctly, that the same intensity redirected would make him a formidable minister.

‘Injurious’ is hubristēs, describing someone whose contempt for others erupts into outrageous, violent acts — not petty rudeness but active cruelty. That’s the raw material grace took hold of.
translation: I have constant gratitude to him who clothed me with strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me trustworthy, appointing me to service — though I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor and a man of violent, outrageous contempt. But I was shown mercy, because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief; and the grace of our Lord overflowed all the more, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

label: 1 Timothy 1:15–17
text:
‘Faithful’ is pistos, a word papyrus letters of the period use for someone reliable enough to trust with money or a message — Paul is staking that same reliability on the sentence he’s about to state as fact.

‘Chief’ translates an intensive pronoun: not that Paul ranks worst among sinners in some cosmic tally, but that he stands, in his own case, foremost — the extreme test case proving Christ’s patience has no ceiling.

That patience is makrothumia, built from ‘long’ and thumos, the word for a violent, seething passion stronger even than ordinary anger — makrothumia is the long, sustained holding-back of that eruption, restraint stretched out over time rather than a single moment of calm.

Paul reaches for ‘eternal,’ not ‘everlasting,’ deliberately: the life given the believer had no beginning, because it’s God’s own life extended to us, while what’s often called ‘everlasting’ punishment has a beginning but supposedly no end — two different shapes of endlessness.

And ‘immortal,’ describing God, is better rendered ‘incorruptible’ — not exemption from death so much as freedom from decay, from any process of wearing down.
translation: Trustworthy is the saying and worthy of full acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am foremost. Yet for this reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display his utmost patience, as an example to those who were going to be believing on him for life eternal. Now to the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

label: 1 Timothy 1:18–20
text:
‘Son’ is teknon, ‘child’ — a term Paul uses as an endearment for grown men too, not a note on Timothy’s age.

‘Put away’ understates the Greek, which is literally ‘thrust from themselves’ — a violent, deliberate shove against one’s own conscience, not a passive drifting.

And ‘faith’ carries the definite article: not their personal trust broken, but the Faith, the body of Christian doctrine, which they wrecked against like a ship.

‘Delivered to Satan’ is a perfect tense — a completed act with a result still standing at the moment Paul writes: Hymenaeus and Alexander are still under that sentence, not merely something Paul once did to them.
translation: This charge I am entrusting to you, child Timothy, in keeping with the prophecies once made about you, so that by them you may be waging the good warfare, holding on to faith and a good conscience — which some, having thrust from themselves, have suffered shipwreck concerning the Faith; among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may be taught not to go on blaspheming.

label: 1 Timothy 2:3–5
text:
‘Our Savior, God’ plays off a title claimed by the reigning Caesar in the imperial cult — ‘savior’ in the sense of the one who held the empire together and kept the peace. Paul sets God’s saviorhood against that: not political preservation but rescue from sin.

‘Will’ is thelō, a wish rooted in desire rather than cold decree — God’s longing that all be saved arises from something like emotion, though it doesn’t override the human will he built into people.

‘Knowledge’ is epignōsis, ‘full’ or precise knowledge, a compound the New Testament reserves for grasping things ethical and divine, never applied to God’s own knowledge.

‘Mediator’ is mesitēs, the technical word for someone who steps between two parties to broker peace or seal a covenant — and the word for ‘man’ here isn’t anēr, a male individual, but anthrōpos, the racial term for humanity. Christ didn’t merely become a man; in taking on anthrōpos, he identified himself with the whole human race.
translation: This is good and acceptable before God our Savior, whose will it is that all people be saved and come into a full, precise knowledge of the truth. For God is one, and there is one mediator between God and mankind — himself mankind, Christ Jesus.

label: 1 Timothy 2:8
text:
‘I will’ switches verbs from the thelō of verse 4 to boulomai — a desire that proceeds from deliberate judgment rather than feeling; Paul isn’t wishing, he’s directing.

‘Holy hands’ uses hosios, not the more common hagios — this is holiness as lived experience, a life actually conformed to what’s right, not positional or ceremonial purity.

And ‘doubting’ is dialogismos, disputatious, skeptical reasoning — the kind of prayer Paul rules out isn’t uncertainty about outcomes but an argumentative, second-guessing spirit turned either on God’s character or on the people being prayed for.
translation: I want, then, the men to be praying in every place, lifting up hands that are holy, apart from anger and skeptical arguing.

label: 1 Timothy 2:13–15
text:
‘Formed’ is plassō, the potter’s word — molding clay or wax by hand, the same verb the Greek Old Testament uses for God shaping Adam from the dust.

Eve’s deception is intensified: Adam simply wasn’t ‘deceived’ (apataō), but Eve was exapataō’d — the compound piles on a prefix meaning ‘thoroughly, completely,’ marking hers as the deeper deception.

‘Was’ in transgression is a perfect tense of ginomai, ‘to become’ — not a static state but a falling into a condition that then held.

And ‘saved’ (sōzō) covers a wide range in the New Testament — healed, rescued from a wreck, kept safe — it isn’t limited to eternal salvation; here, describing a woman Paul has already assumed to be a believer, the sense is being kept safe and brought through, not converted, in the ordinary work of childbearing.
translation: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been thoroughly deceived, came to be in transgression. Yet she will be kept safe through her childbearing, if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with sound judgment.

label: 1 Timothy 3:2
text:
‘Blameless’ compounds ‘to lay hold of’ with a negating alpha — literally ‘un-grabbable’: a life with no handle on it for accusation to catch.

‘Husband of one wife’ is, word for word, ‘a one-woman man’ — both nouns lack the definite article, a Greek construction that emphasizes quality of character over bare fact.

It’s less a marital headcount than a description of temperament: a man whose love, by nature, fixes on one woman, the way we’d call a dog ‘a one-man dog’ to describe its loyalty, not its history.

‘Vigilant’ (nēphalios) pictures someone calm, level-headed, and clear-eyed rather than simply sober from drink.

‘Hospitable’ compounds ‘fond of’ with ‘stranger’ — literally someone drawn toward the outsider, the traveler, the person with no other place to go.
translation: The overseer, then, must be a man on whom nothing can be laid hold of — a one-woman kind of man, level-headed, sound-minded, orderly, hospitable to the stranger, skilled at teaching.

label: 1 Timothy 3:3
text:
‘Not given to wine’ compounds ‘wine’ with ‘beside’ — one who lingers too long at the cup and turns quarrelsome under it.

‘No striker’ is literally ‘a bruiser,’ someone quick with a fist.

‘Patient’ is epieikēs, a word better rendered ‘sweetly reasonable’ — someone who won’t press his legal rights to their absolute limit even when he’s entitled to, because strict justice pushed too far becomes its own injustice.

‘No brawler’ builds on machē, ‘battle’ — not a man who goes looking for a fight.

And ‘not covetous’ is literally ‘not fond of silver.’
translation: Not one who lingers over wine and turns quarrelsome, not a striker, but sweetly reasonable, not a fighter, not a lover of silver.

label: 1 Timothy 3:6
text:
‘Novice’ is neophutos, ‘newly sprung up’ — the word used of a palm tree just planted, roots not yet down.

‘Lifted up with pride’ is tuphoō, literally ‘to raise smoke’ — pride here isn’t just inflation but a fog that clouds the mind, leaving a man stupefied by his own self-regard, unable to see straight.

And ‘condemnation’ (krima) is the specific judicial sentence under which the devil already stands, the verdict passed on him for the original sin of pride — precisely the trap Paul warns a hasty appointment could walk a new believer into.
translation: Not a newly planted one, lest, being clouded with the smoke of pride, he fall into the condemnation of the devil.

label: 1 Timothy 3:7
text: ‘Good report’ is marturia kalē, an ‘excellent testimony’ — Paul wants the outside world’s read on this man’s character to be positive, not merely the church’s, on the theory that outsider opinion can catch what insider loyalty misses.
translation: It is also necessary that he have an excellent testimony from those outside, so that he not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.

label: 1 Timothy 3:10
text:
‘Proved’ is dokimazō — testing aimed at approval, the assumption being the candidate passes.

‘Blameless’ is anegklētoi, a courtroom word: ‘unaccused,’ no charge standing against him.

The participle carrying it is conditional in force — ‘let them serve, provided they remain unaccused’ — approval isn’t a one-time hurdle but an ongoing state.
translation: And let these also first be tested; then let them serve as deacons, provided they are found unaccused.

label: 1 Timothy 3:11
text:
‘Wives’ has no possessive pronoun in the Greek and simply reads ‘women’ — likely a third office in this list (the connective hōsautōs, ‘likewise,’ is Paul’s marker for adding another item in a series), women deacons such as Phoebe in Romans 16, not the spouses of the men just described.

‘Slanderers’ is diabolos, the very word used elsewhere for ‘the devil’ — from a verb meaning ‘to throw across, to falsely accuse’; a slanderer does, in miniature, exactly what Satan’s name describes him doing at large.
translation: Women, likewise, must be dignified, not slanderers, level-headed, faithful in all things.

label: 1 Timothy 3:16
text:
‘Without controversy’ is homologoumenōs, ‘confessedly’ — everyone concedes the point, from the verb ‘to agree with.’

‘Manifest in the flesh’ uses phaneroō, ‘made visible’: the invisible one becomes visible, not by acquiring existence but by taking on a body that could be seen.

‘Justified in the Spirit’ doesn’t use dikaioō in its usual sense of a sinner declared righteous — here it means vindicated, endorsed, proved to be what he claimed. The whole line balances flesh against spirit: flesh is his humanity, openly on display; spirit is his deity, usually cloaked beneath that humanity but breaking through at moments like the Transfiguration, each such moment vindicating who he really was.

‘Received up’ translates the technical term Luke uses for the ascension itself in Acts 1.
translation: And confessedly great is the mystery of godliness: he was made visible in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

label: 1 Timothy 4:6
text:
‘Brethren’ is adelphos, literally ‘from the same womb’ — Christians as a single family sharing one Father.

‘Put in remembrance’ is a milder verb than direct exhortation, literally ‘to put under,’ i.e. to suggest, to plant an idea rather than hammer it home.

‘Minister’ is diakonos, emphasizing activity rather than office — a servant seen in the act of serving, not yet the technical title ‘clergyman’ it would later become.

‘Nourished up’ is a present participle: not a meal once eaten but continual feeding, an ongoing diet.

And ‘attained’ is a perfect tense — ‘have closely followed and still hold the results,’ a finished course of instruction whose effect persists into the present.
translation: By constantly putting these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, continually nourishing yourself on the words of the faith and of the good teaching which you have closely followed and now hold.

label: 1 Timothy 4:9–11
text:
‘Labor’ (kopiaō) means work to the point of exhaustion; its partner is agōnizomai, the word for competing in the Greek games, the root of our ‘agony’ — together they picture strenuous, painful effort, not casual service.

‘Trust’ is a perfect tense of elpizō: ‘we have set our hope,’ with the sense that the hope, once fixed, now stands settled and fixed in place.

Calling God ‘Savior of all men, especially of believers’ plays on two senses of the word at once — he is Savior of everyone in that he has provided salvation available to all at the cross, but Savior in the fullest, realized sense only for those who’ve actually placed their faith in it.
translation: This saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For it is to this end that we labor to exhaustion and are contending, because we have set, and still have set, our hope on the living God, who is Savior of all men, especially of those who believe. These things keep commanding and teaching.

label: 1 Timothy 4:12
text:
‘Despise’ isn’t a passive feeling — kataphroneō is contempt that shows itself in action, and the prohibition is a present imperative, which in Greek forbids the continuing of something already underway: Paul isn’t warning against a hypothetical, he’s telling Timothy to stop letting a thing that’s already happening keep happening.

‘Be’ an example is likewise not the ordinary verb ‘to be’ but ginomai, ‘to become’ — ‘keep on becoming,’ an ongoing process rather than a fixed state achieved once.

‘Example’ is tupos, the mark left by a blow or the impression stamped by a die — the pattern other lives get shaped against, not just a good instance among many.
translation: Stop letting anyone look down on your youth, but keep on becoming a pattern for the believers, in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.

label: 1 Timothy 4:13
text:
‘Reading’ is anagnōsis, technical for the public reading of Scripture aloud in the gathered assembly, sometimes with running comment attached.

‘Give attendance to’ is prosechō, literally ‘hold toward’ — keep your mind fastened on this. The order Paul lists — reading, then exhortation, then teaching — likely reflects logical priority as much as sequence: exhortation needs teaching under it as a foundation, so instruction has to come first even where exhortation is named first.
translation: Until I come, keep holding your attention on the public reading, on exhortation, on teaching.

label: 1 Timothy 4:14
text:
‘Gift’ is charisma, Paul’s technical term for a Spirit-given capacity that equips someone for a specific service in the church, not a natural talent but a direct impartation.

It came ‘through prophecy’ — prophetic words spoken over Timothy, apparently repeated at his ordination when the elders (presbuterion, the formal body of elders) laid hands on him, an act of identification marking him as now one of their number.

‘Do not neglect’ is a present imperative in a prohibition, which in Greek forbids continuing something already in motion — Timothy, by temperament diffident, seems to have actually been letting this gift go unused, and Paul is telling him to stop.
translation: Do not keep neglecting the gift that is in you, which was given you through prophecy, along with the laying on of the hands of the elders.

label: 1 Timothy 4:15
text:
‘Meditate’ is meletaō, the word for an orator’s rehearsal — not quiet reflection but active practice, drilling a skill.

‘Give yourself wholly to them’ is literally ‘be constantly in these things’ — total immersion, not periodic attention.

And ‘profiting’ is prokopē, ‘to cut forward’ — a pioneer’s word for blazing a trail through brush no one has cleared yet, picturing Timothy’s growth as visible, forward progress rather than passive maturing.
translation: Practice these things; be constantly in them, so that your advance may be evident to all.

label: 1 Timothy 4:16
text:
‘Take heed’ is epechō, literally ‘to hold upon’ — fasten your attention and don’t let go.

‘Continue’ is epimenō, ‘to stay by the side of’ something, sticking close rather than checking in occasionally.

The ‘salvation’ in view can’t be the sinner’s conversion or the saint’s preservation, since both of those are God’s work, not the fruit of careful teaching; given the immediate context about demon-inspired error, it’s rescue from getting tangled in false doctrine — Timothy protects himself and his hearers from heresy by staying glued to the reading, exhortation, and teaching of the Word.
translation: Keep holding your attention on yourself and on the teaching. Stay right by these things — for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who are listening to you.

label: 1 Timothy 5:3
text:
‘Honor’ is timao, ‘to fix the value of’ something and then pay it the respect that value warrants — here the context folds in the practical sense of financial support as part of that honor.

‘Widows indeed’ uses ontōs, ‘truly, genuinely’ — Paul is marking off a specific class: women left completely without family support, as the following verses go on to define.
translation: Be constantly showing honor to widows who are truly widows.

label: 1 Timothy 5:4
text:
‘Show piety’ is eusebeō, the same root elsewhere translated ‘godliness’ — Paul treats family duty as itself an act of reverence, not a separate category from religion.

‘At home’ is literally ‘their own private household’ (idios doubling down on ‘own’), marking this as a family obligation before it’s a church one.

‘Requite’ is apodidōmi, ‘to give off from oneself’ — the image is of discharging a debt, throwing off a weight one owes, rather than doing a favor.

And ‘parents’ translates progonos, literally ‘those who came into being before’ — broader than just mother and father, covering grandparents and forebears generally.
translation: But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own household and to discharge what they owe their forebears — for this is pleasing in the sight of God.

label: 1 Timothy 5:5–7
text:
‘Desolate’ is a perfect participle of a verb meaning ‘left utterly alone’ — not just presently by herself but settled into that condition.

‘Trusteth’ is a perfect tense of elpizō, ‘to hope’: a past act whose result has become permanent, so ‘has fixed her hope, and it stays fixed.’

‘Liveth in pleasure’ translates a verb closer to ‘lives wastefully, wantonly’ — squandering rather than merely enjoying.

And the line about being ‘dead while she liveth’ pairs a present participle (‘living’) with a perfect verb (‘has died’): she is living, having died, with the abiding result that she is, right now, a dead woman walking.
translation: But the widow who has been left utterly alone has fixed her hope on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day. But the one who lives wastefully — she is living, having died, so that she is dead. Keep commanding these things as well, so that they may be beyond reproach.

label: 1 Timothy 5:8
text:
‘Provide’ is pronoeō, literally ‘to think of in advance’ — providing here starts with foresight, not just handing over money when asked.

‘Infidel’ is apistos, built by negating pistos, ‘faith’ — the very word for ‘unbeliever.’ Paul’s point bites: a man who won’t do what even an unbeliever does by natural instinct has, in practice, denied the faith he claims — faith that produces no natural fruit isn’t functioning as faith at all.
translation: But if anyone does not think ahead for his own, and especially for those of his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

label: 1 Timothy 5:13
text:
‘Wandering about’ is perierchomai, the word for aimless strollers and wanderers.

‘Tattlers’ is phluareō, ‘to talk nonsense’ — and pointedly, to bring false, idle charges against someone.

‘Busybodies’ is periergos, the same word used in Acts 19 for the ‘curious arts’ of pagan sorcery — prying into what’s concealed, meddling in business that isn’t theirs.
translation: And at the same time they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house — and not only idle, but talkers of nonsense and prying into others’ affairs, saying what they ought not to say.

label: 1 Timothy 5:16
text: ‘Church’ (ekklēsia) is built on ‘to call out from’ — a body summoned out of the general population into an assembly. Paul’s point turns on the word’s plain meaning: family obligations exist precisely so the called-out assembly isn’t burdened with debts that belong to a household first.
translation: If any believer has widows, let him keep assisting them, and let the assembly not be burdened, so that it may assist those who are truly widows.

label: 1 Timothy 5:19
text:
‘Accusation’ is katēgoria, specifically a formal charge brought before a tribunal — not gossip or complaint, a legal-sounding word.

And ‘before’ two or three witnesses is epi, ‘upon’ — the charge must stand upon their authority, requiring their testimony as its actual basis rather than mere hearsay.
translation: Against an elder, do not accept an accusation except upon the testimony of two or three witnesses.

label: 1 Timothy 5:20
text:
‘Rebuke’ is elegchō — not a scolding but the wielding of truth with such force that it brings the guilty party to an actual conviction of the wrong, whether or not he confesses it.

‘Others’ who are meant to fear are specifically ‘the rest’ of the elders, hoi loipoi — this is a check aimed at the leadership class itself.
translation: Those who are sinning, keep rebuking in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear.

label: 1 Timothy 5:21
text:
‘I charge’ is diamarturomai, a classical word for calling gods and men to witness a solemn testimony — the strongest form of adjuration available, which tells us something about how seriously Paul needed Timothy to take this.

The Greek grammar behind ‘God, and the Lord Jesus Christ’ actually identifies the two as one: ‘our God, even Christ Jesus’ — a direct, pointed claim of Christ’s deity, aimed like a spear at the imperial cult that called Caesar ‘lord’ and ‘god.’
translation: I solemnly charge you before our God, even Christ Jesus, and the elect angels, that you guard these things without prejudging, doing nothing out of favoritism.

label: 1 Timothy 5:22
text:
Laying on hands signals identification — restoring the repentant sinner back into visible fellowship with the assembly, not a ritual gesture.

‘Keep’ is tēreō, watchful, ongoing custody — the verb assumes you already possess the thing you’re guarding.

And ‘pure’ here is hagnos in the sense of ‘upright, honorable,’ not narrowly ‘chaste’ — Paul’s concern is Timothy’s integrity in these restoration decisions broadly, not just sexual purity.
translation: Lay hands hastily on no one, and do not share in the sins of others. Keep watchful guard over yourself, staying pure.

label: 1 Timothy 5:23
text: ‘Drink no longer water’ is really ‘stop being a water-drinker’ — Timothy’s habit, not a single glass, and Paul isn’t banning water so much as prescribing wine as medicine for a specific ailment. The word for wine, oinos, means the fermented drink throughout, not a modern grape-juice substitute — Paul is recommending a period remedy, not laying down a beverage policy.
translation: No longer be a water-drinker only, but be using a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.

label: 1 Timothy 5:24
text: ‘Open beforehand’ misreads the pro- prefix as a time marker; it’s actually just intensifying — ‘openly manifest to all eyes,’ plainly obvious, not ‘obvious ahead of time.’ Paul pictures some sins marching ahead of the sinner like heralds, announcing the verdict before any court convenes, while other sins trail behind, only surfacing at the judgment itself.
translation: The sins of some people are openly manifest, going ahead to judgment; the sins of others, they follow after.

label: 1 Timothy 5:25
text:
‘Likewise’ signals an antithesis, not a repetition: just as some sins are plain and some stay hidden until judgment, so some good works are obvious and some aren’t — but even the hidden good can’t stay hidden forever.

‘Otherwise’ doesn’t mean ‘bad’; it means ‘not yet visible.’
translation: In the same way, good works too are openly manifest; and those that are not, are not able to remain hidden.

label: 1 Timothy 6:2
text:
‘Despise’ is kataphroneō, ‘to think down on’ — contempt shown in dismissive treatment.

The verb for ‘do them service’ shares its root with doulos, ‘slave’ — literally ‘slave for them all the more.’

‘Faithful’ here doesn’t describe a virtue but a status: pistos means ‘believers,’ brothers in the faith, not simply ‘trustworthy.’

And ‘benefit’ is euergesia in its ordinary secular sense of ‘kindly service’ — the kind acts these Christian masters do for their slaves, not favors the slaves owe back.
translation: And those who have believing masters, let them not look down on them because they are brothers, but let them serve them all the more, because those who benefit by their work are believers and beloved.

label: 1 Timothy 6:3–5
text:
‘Wholesome’ teaching is again hugiainō, ‘healthy’ — Paul keeps this whole letter’s controversy in medical terms, sound doctrine versus disease.

‘Proud’ is tuphoo, the same ‘smoke-blinded’ word from 3:6, here in the perfect tense: not a passing flare of ego but a settled, permanent fog.

‘Knowing nothing’ is epistamai plus ‘not even one thing’ — total incapacity for real, fixed thought, not mere ignorance of facts.

And ‘destitute of the truth’ is apostereo, ‘defrauded, robbed’ — the tense implies they once actually held the truth and have since been stripped of it, whether by their own doing or another’s.
translation: If anyone teaches otherwise and does not agree with the healthy words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that fits godliness, he has been permanently clouded with pride, understanding not even one thing, but sick with a craving for controversies and word-battles, out of which come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among men whose minds have been robbed of the truth, who reckon godliness a means of gain.

label: 1 Timothy 6:6–10
text:
‘Contentment’ is autarkeia, a Stoic technical term for inward self-sufficiency — needing nothing from outside circumstances to stay steady.

The logic linking verses 6 and 7 runs on ‘because,’ not ‘and’: we brought nothing in because we can carry nothing out, one fact proving the other.

The ‘content’ of verse 8 shares that root but drops the ‘self’ prefix — arkeo, ‘to have unfailing strength against a threat,’ the same word behind ‘my grace is sufficient for thee.’

‘Will be rich’ uses boulomai, the reasoned, deliberated desire, not a passing impulse — this is calculated ambition, not a stray temptation.

And ‘coveted’ is orego, ‘to stretch oneself out to grasp something,’ the same reaching gesture used positively elsewhere of desiring a good work — here bent toward money instead.
translation: But godliness with self-sufficiency is great gain, because we brought nothing into the world, since we are not able to carry anything out either; and having food and covering, with these we shall be sufficiently strengthened. But those who have settled on wanting to be rich fall into temptation and a trap and many senseless and harmful cravings, which plunge men into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all the evils; reaching for it, some have been led away from the faith and have pierced themselves through with many consuming griefs.

label: 1 Timothy 6:11
text:
‘But thou’ emphatically sets Timothy apart from the money-lovers just described — ‘you, in contrast to them.’

‘Flee’ is a present imperative: not a single dash for the exit but a lifelong habit of continual fleeing.

‘Follow’ (diōkō) is the same verb for a hunter’s pursuit, running hard after something desired.

And ‘patience’ is hupomonē, built from ‘remain’ and ‘under’ — literally the stance of remaining under a weight rather than throwing it off, endurance as a settled posture, not a single act of grit.
translation: But you, man of God, keep fleeing from these things; and keep pursuing righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patient endurance, gentleness.

label: 1 Timothy 6:12
text:
‘Fight’ is agōnizomai, a present imperative — the ongoing, no-let-up struggle of the Greek athletic games, not a single skirmish.

‘Good’ is kalos, not agathos — goodness as a spectator sees it, the beauty of technique on display, not just moral rightness.

‘Lay hold’ switches to an aorist imperative, viewing the habitual grasping-after eternal life as one decisive, summed-up act rather than a process — Timothy already has eternal life as a gift; Paul is urging him to grip it, to lay hold of what it means in experience, not to acquire it for the first time.
translation: Keep fighting the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and about which you spoke the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

label: 1 Timothy 6:13–16
text:
‘Quickeneth’ is zōogoneō, ‘preserves alive’ — Timothy is reminded he answers to the One who keeps everything, including him, in existence.

‘Keep’ the commandment is an aorist imperative, a sharp, military-style order given all at once, fitting for a Paul who knew Timothy’s naturally hesitant temperament needed a jolt now and then.

‘Appearing’ is epiphaneia, the word pagan Greek used for a god’s glorious manifestation to help his people — Paul redirects it to Christ’s return.

‘Times’ is kairos, not chronos — not clock-time but God’s own strategically appointed seasons, known to him alone.

And ‘immortality’ is athanasia, built by simply negating ‘death’ — ‘no-death,’ the flat opposite of what every mortal faces, reserved here for God alone.
translation: I charge you, in the presence of God who is constantly keeping all things alive, and of Christ Jesus who testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate: keep this command spotless, beyond reproach, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he will show at his own appointed seasons — he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords, who alone has no-death, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or is able to see. To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.

label: 1 Timothy 6:17–19
text:
‘World’ is aiōn, literally ‘the now age’ — not the physical globe but the whole floating atmosphere of values and assumptions people currently breathe, the present age’s spirit rather than kosmos, the ordered universe.

‘High-minded’ compounds ‘think’ with ‘high’ — thinking of oneself as elevated.

‘Trust’ uses a perfect infinitive of elpizō: ‘have set, and still have, their hope fixed’ on wealth’s instability rather than on God.

And ‘giveth’ is parechō, ‘holds forth, continually offers’ — God as the one perpetually extending good things for enjoyment, not a distant benefactor but an active, ongoing giver.
translation: Charge those who are rich in the present age not to be high-minded, nor to have set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who is constantly holding out to us all things richly to enjoy — to be doing good, to be rich in good works, generous, ready to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of what is truly life.
